newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bond futures slipped slightly on Friday under pressure from the U.S. market but traders remained confident the market would pick up again next week despite the risk of short-term set backs.

Some analysts were less optimistic on the grounds that even though the underlying picture of weak European growth, combined with fading concerns about the strength of the U.S. economy, would help, markets had already priced in much of the good news.
The most striking move on Friday was the continued decline of the franc, along with the mark, against the dollar. It fell as low as 5.4510, the lowest since December 30, 1994.

"Next week should be bullish. Our target is 131," Valerie Plagnol, market economist at Credit Commercial de France said. She said the U.S. data next week should not cause any upheavals and the trend in Europe remained one of slowing economic growth.
These two factors, combined with the climb of the dollar, should continue to favour the market, she said.

Another trader said the market was reassured by the decline in the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index in January, which was released after a stronger-than-expected rise in U.S. December industrial production.
The head of trading at a French brokerage said, "It's still a bull market in the long term even if there is the possibility of a correction in the short term."

Another trader at a large French brokerage said there was some profit taking after the U.S. production figures but he said, "There are not many sellers of the notionnel (French bond future)...We're on the way to see 131."

The March bond future settled at 130.46, down 0.16 on the day. It found good support in the 130.28/34 zone but failed to push beyond resistance above 130.50. The all-time high, hit on January 13, 1994 at 131.38, remained the major target.
International economist Sean Shepley said while he supported the underlying arguments which favoured lower yields in Europe, the risks of a decline in bond prices were growing.
"It can carry on for a bit more, the markets have quite a bit of momentum -- and its hard to see what can trigger the correction," Shepley said.

"But rather than just pricing in what's happened, the markets are pricing in an acceleration in (European) economic weakness. The European economy is not as weak as the beginning of last year, there has been a policy easing and exports are picking up," he said.

He said while there was no serious risk of inflation picking up in Europe and that the rise in the dollar against the mark was favourable for European exports, "the chances of (Buba) easing during such a period of mark weakness is very low."
The 10-year spread between French and German benchmark bonds, using the October 2006 OAT and the January 2007 Bund, remained stable at minus 15 basis points.
March PIBOR was also unchanged at 96.80 while the June contract climbed slightly to 96.85.
